lessons.title: Python basics for a C++ coder
lessons.intro: Your logic stays the same. Only the syntax changes: no semicolons, no braces, no types. Indentation is the block.
map: a // b                # floor division; a / b gives a float

code.title: Numbers, loops, functions
code.src:
n = 7
print(n // 2, n % 2, n / 2)     # floor division, remainder, true division
print(2 ** 100)                 # no overflow, ever
a, b = 3, 5
a, b = b, a                     # swap in one line
print(a, b)
for i in range(5, 0, -1):       # 5 down to 1
    print(i, end=' ')
print()
total = 0
for x in [4, 8, 15]:
    total += x
print(f"total = {total}")       # f-string: values inside {}

def add(x, y=10):               # y has a default value
    return x + y
print(add(5), add(5, 1))
if total > 20 and not total % 2:
    print("big and even")
elif total > 20:
    print("big and odd")

watch: Indentation is the block. Use 4 spaces, the same everywhere; a wrong indent is an error or a bug.
`/` always gives a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Use `//` for integer division.
`range(a, b)` stops before `b`, exactly like `i < b`.

quiz.why: `//` is integer division, `/` always returns a float.

quiz.why: Start 1, step 3, stop before 10.
Python has no `++`. `++x` is just plus-plus-x, so it stays 5, and x is not changed.

quiz.code:

a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)
quiz.why: The right side is computed first with the old values (2, 1 + 2), then assigned.

lessons.title: Lists: the dynamic array (your vector)
lessons.intro: A Python list is a C++ vector: one block of memory holding references, which grows by itself when it fills up.
map: v.sort()              # sorted(v) returns a new list
b = a[:]   or   b = a.copy()     # b = a is NOT a copy

code.title: Everyday list work
code.src:
v = [5, 2, 9]
v.append(4)              # [5, 2, 9, 4]
v.insert(0, 7)           # [7, 5, 2, 9, 4]
last = v.pop()           # removes and returns 4
print(v, last, len(v), v[-1])
print(v[1:3], v[:2], v[::-1])     # slices are new lists
v.sort()

print()

c = a[:]       # a real copy

code.title: How the dynamic array grows
code.note: Your numbers can differ by Python version. The point: memory grows in jumps, so append is amortized O(1), like vector::push_back.
code.src:
import sys
v = []
last = sys.getsizeof(v)
print(f"len={len(v):2}  bytes={last}")
for i in range(20):
    v.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(v)
    if size != last:              # only print when the list had to grow
        print(f"len={len(v):2}  bytes={size}")
        last = size

len= 1  bytes=88
len= 5  bytes=120

len=17  bytes=248

code.title: Build your own dynamic array (the interview answer)
code.note: Classes come properly in lesson 10; here, just follow the idea. A fixed block fills up, a block twice as big is made, everything is copied over. Copying is O(n) but happens rarely, so append is O(1) on average (amortized).
code.out:
added 10: size 1, capacity 1
added 20: size 2, capacity 2
added 30: size 3, capacity 4
added 40: size 4, capacity 4
added 50: size 5, capacity 8
50

watch: A list stores references in one block of memory. When it is full, Python allocates a bigger block (about 1.125 times plus a little) and copies, so `append` and `pop()` are O(1) on average.
`pop(0)` and `insert(0, x)` shift every element: O(n). For a queue use `collections.deque` (lesson 7).
`v.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Never write `v = v.sort()`.

quiz.why: `b = a` gives the same list a second name. Copy with `a[:]`.
Slice from index 1 up to, but not including, 4.
`.sort()` changes the list and returns None. `sorted()` returns a new list.
Negative indexes count from the end; `[::-1]` is a reversed copy.

lessons.title: Hashing: dict, set, Counter
lessons.intro: dict is your unordered_map and set is your unordered_set. Counter and defaultdict remove most of the counting boilerplate.
map: m[k] = m.get(k, 0) + 1   or   cnt[k] += 1 with Counter
sorted(m.items())   when you need the order
(a, b)   a tuple; tuples can be dict keys, lists cannot

code.title: Counting and grouping
code.src:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
nums = [3, 1, 3, 2, 3, 1]
freq = {}
for x in nums:
    freq[x] = freq.get(x, 0) + 1
print(freq)
cnt = Counter(nums)
print(cnt[3], cnt[7], cnt.most_common(2))
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat"]:
    groups[tuple(sorted(w))].append(w)
print(list(groups.values()))
seen = set()
for x in nums:
    if x in seen:
        print("first repeat:", x)
        break
    seen.add(x)
print({1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}, {1, 2} | {5}, {1, 2, 3} - {2})
m = {"b": 2, "a": 5, "c": 1}
print(sorted(m), sorted(m.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]), max(m, key=m.get))

code.title: Two Sum with a dict

watch: `m[k]` on a missing key raises KeyError. Use `m.get(k, 0)`, `k in m`, or a defaultdict.
Only immutable things can be keys: numbers, strings, tuples. Turn a list into a tuple first.
Since Python 3.7 a dict keeps insertion order. It is still not sorted; use `sorted()`.

quiz.why: .get returns the default when the key is missing.

drill.task: Count subarrays whose sum equals k, using prefix sums and a dict (LeetCode 560).
drill.src:
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1
    total = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen[total - k]
        seen[total] += 1
    return count

lessons.intro: heapq gives you a priority queue, `key=` replaces comparators, and bisect gives you lower_bound and upper_bound.

code.title: Heaps
code.src:
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print(h[0], heapq.heappop(h), heapq.heappop(h))     # smallest first
maxh = [-x for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]]
heapq.heapify(maxh)
print(-heapq.heappop(maxh))                          # max-heap trick
print(heapq.nlargest(2, [5, 1, 8, 3]), heapq.nsmallest(2, [5, 1, 8, 3]))
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write"))                  # tuples compare by first item
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "read"))
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))

code.title: Sorting with keys and comparators, and binary search
code.src:
people = [("amit", 25), ("riya", 22), ("dev", 25)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))   # age high to low, then name
intervals = [[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6]]
intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])
print(intervals)
from functools import cmp_to_key
nums = [3, 30, 34, 5, 9]
nums.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda x, y: -1 if str(x) + str(y) > str(y) + str(x) else 1))
print("".join(map(str, nums)))                       # largest number
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
a = [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7]
print(bisect_left(a, 4), bisect_right(a, 4), bisect_left(a, 5))

def lower_bound(a, x):            # the same thing by hand
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo
print(lower_bound(a, 4), lower_bound(a, 8))

watch: heapq is always a min-heap. For a max-heap push `-x`; for pairs push `(-key, value)`.
A comparator for `cmp_to_key` returns a negative number, 0 or a positive number, not True/False like C++.
`(lo + hi) // 2` cannot overflow in Python, so you do not need `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.

quiz.why: heapify makes a min-heap; the smallest is at index 0.
key=len sorts by length.
The first index whose value is at least 4 is index 2.
reverse=True sorts high to low.

lessons.title: Recursion, backtracking and memo
lessons.intro: Recursion is written the same way. The Python-specific parts are copying the path into the answer, `nonlocal`, and `@cache` for memoisation.
map: nonlocal counter   inside a nested function
deep recursion is fine in C++

code.title: Subsets and permutations
code.src:
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])          # copy, because path keeps changing
            return
        path.append(nums[i])             # take nums[i]
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.pop()                       # undo
        dfs(i + 1)                       # skip nums[i]
    dfs(0)
    return res
print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))

def permutations(nums):
    res, path, used = [], [], [False] * len(nums)
    def dfs():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = True
                path.append(nums[i])
                dfs()
                path.pop()
                used[i] = False
    dfs()
    return res
print(permutations([1, 2, 3]))

code.title: Memo with @cache, nonlocal, and the recursion limit

watch: `res.append(path)` stores a reference: every entry ends up as the same final list. Append `path[:]`.
Assigning to an outer variable inside a nested function needs `nonlocal`, or you get UnboundLocalError. Changing a list with `.append` does not.
Never use a mutable default like `def f(x, acc=[])`: the same list is shared between calls.

quiz.why: res holds a reference to path, which changed afterwards.

quiz.code:
def outer():
    c = 0
    def inc():
        c += 1
    inc()
    return c
print(outer())
quiz.why: Assigning to c inside inc makes it local there. Add `nonlocal c`.

quiz.code:
def f(a, acc=[]):
    acc.append(a)
    return acc
f(1)
print(f(2))
quiz.why: The default list is created once and shared by every call.

lessons.intro: The last day: the differences that cause wrong answers, how to print and read fast, and a 45-minute mock in Python only.
map: never happens (but huge numbers are slower)
b = a  shares; copy with a[:]

code.title: Differences that give wrong answers
code.src:
print(-7 // 2, int(-7 / 2), -7 % 3)
arr = [3, 1, 2]
print(*arr)
print(*arr, sep=",")

x = 0.1 + 0.2

import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
nums = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
print(sum(nums))

code.title: A "complete the function" question
code.src:
def solution(arr):
    # Return the second largest distinct value, or -1 if there is none.
    distinct = sorted(set(arr), reverse=True)
    return distinct[1] if len(distinct) > 1 else -1
print(solution([4, 9, 2, 9, 7]), solution([5, 5]))

watch: Many online assessments give you a function to complete; others read from standard input. Practise both forms before your test.
`round()` rounds halves to the even number: `round(2.5)` is 2. If the question says round half up, use `int(x + 0.5)` for positive numbers.
Python is slower than C++. Prefer built-ins (`sum`, `max`, `sorted`, `Counter`) over hand-written loops when the limits are big.

drill.task: Read T test cases from standard input. Each has n and then n numbers. Print the largest number of each test case.
drill.src:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
t = int(data[0])
i = 1
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(data[i]); i += 1
    arr = list(map(int, data[i:i + n])); i += n
    print(max(arr))
